claims.text: Adding specific alloying elements to metals can enhance ductility.
Pure iron and pure copper have low ductility.
Nickel or manganese can be alloyed with a base metal to increase its ductility.
The proposed ductility enhancement applies under standard atmospheric conditions and temperatures typical of metal processing.
Grain structure and phase distribution mediate the effect of alloying on ductility.
Adding alloying elements modifies the metal's microstructure.
The alloying-induced microstructural changes improve available slip systems and dislocation movement.
Improved slip systems and dislocation movement enhance ductility.
The alloyed metal will have greater ductility than the corresponding pure metal.
The alloyed metal will exhibit a higher elongation percentage before fracture than the pure metal.
Pure iron has approximately 15% elongation before fracture.
The magnitude of the ductility increase depends on the identities and concentrations of the alloying elements.

contradictions.description: The general hypothesis says alloying can enhance ductility, which is an existential or conditional claim, whereas the falsification rule rejects it if any tested nickel- or manganese-alloyed sample fails to exceed pure iron. A single unsuccessful composition does not logically falsify the broader claim that some alloying additions or concentrations can enhance ductility.
